match.reason: The bank point defines corporate culture and its effect on morale and turnover, but it does not teach managers building a culture that welcomes change through shared values, rewards, stories and their own example, so it is related rather than the same idea.

draft.title: Developing corporate culture
card: Corporate culture is the shared values, beliefs and ways of behaving in a business. It shapes how staff act when no one is watching, including how they react to change.
Shared values
Managers can state values such as openness to new ideas and use them in hiring, meetings and decisions, so staff know what the business cares about.
Rewards and stories
Managers can reward staff who suggest or adopt new ways of working. They can retell stories of past changes that went well, which shows others what is valued.
Own example
Staff watch what managers do. When managers follow the values themselves, such as trying a new system first, staff are more likely to follow.
draft.remember: Culture is built by what managers say, reward, retell and do themselves.

a.q: Which action by a manager most directly builds a culture that welcomes change?
opts: Rewarding staff who suggest better ways to work
Telling staff to follow the old rules without question
Keeping plans secret until a change takes effect
Asking staff to avoid mistakes by not trying new things
a.why: Rewards show staff that new ideas are valued, so they are more likely to offer and accept them. Keeping plans secret does not build shared values, and it tends to leave staff unprepared for change.
a.clue: Which action shows staff that new ideas are wanted?

b.q: Priya manages a Geelong bakery chain that has bought new ordering software. She tells staff that learning new methods matters, but she keeps using paper orders herself. Why is her approach unlikely to build a culture that welcomes change?
opts: Her own behaviour does not match the values she states
Managers should not state values to staff at all
Staff only change when they receive a pay rise
Culture can only be changed by replacing all staff
b.why: Staff watch what managers do, so Priya's paper orders send a stronger message than her words. Pay rewards can help, but the card shows that example, values, stories and rewards all shape culture, and staff do not all need replacing.
b.clue: Compare what Priya says with what she does.

a.best: Rewarding staff who suggest better ways to work

b.best: Her own behaviour does not match the values she states

problems.detail: Two distractors use 'only' ('Culture can only be changed…', 'Staff only change…') and a third says 'not … at all'. The card uses 'can', and the right option is the only one without absolute wording, so a student can pick it by elimination without knowing the idea.

All three distractors plainly discourage change (avoid trying new things, keep plans secret, follow old rules without question). The question is too easy for Year 12 and does not test understanding of how culture is built.

proposal.title: Developing corporate culture
card: Corporate culture is the shared values, beliefs and ways of behaving in a business. It shapes how staff act when no one is watching, including how they react to change.
Shared values
Managers can state values such as openness to new ideas and use them in hiring, meetings and decisions, so staff know what the business cares about.
Rewards and stories
Managers can reward staff who suggest or adopt new ways of working. They can retell stories of past changes that went well, which shows others what is valued.
Own example
Staff watch what managers do. When managers follow the values themselves, such as trying a new system first, staff are more likely to follow.
proposal.remember: Culture is built by what managers say, reward, retell and do themselves.

a.q: At each staff meeting, a Ballarat hotel manager recounts how a past switch to online check-in won new guests. Which way of building culture is she using?
opts: Retelling stories of past changes that went well
Rewarding staff who adopt new ways of working
Setting an example by trying a new system first
Using stated values to guide hiring decisions
a.why: Recounting a past change that worked is a story, which shows staff what the business values. It is not a reward, because no staff member receives anything for adopting a new method.
a.clue: Is she giving something, doing something, or telling something?

b.q: Priya manages a Geelong bakery chain that has bought new ordering software. She tells staff that learning new methods matters, but she keeps using paper orders herself. Why is her approach unlikely to build a culture that welcomes change?
opts: Her own behaviour does not match the values she states
She stated a value instead of retelling a past success
Culture is shaped by systems rather than by managers
Stating values tends to make staff resist new methods
b.why: Staff watch what managers do, so Priya's paper orders send a stronger message than her words. Stories are one way to build culture, but they are not required, and her stated value fails because her own example contradicts it.
b.clue: Compare what Priya says with what she does.

a.best: Retelling stories of past changes that went well

b.best: Her own behaviour does not match the values she states
